newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Britain's Brown pushes new jobs plan for EU.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Britain's Brown pushes new jobs plan for EU.

text.p: Britain's finance minister Gordon Brown unveiled a new employment plan for Europe on Wednesday, promising to make it a central theme of London's presidency of the European Union next year.
In an effort to put his government at the EU's helm, Chancellor of the Exchequer Brown said he would push a three-point job creation plan at next week's regular meeting of EU finance ministers.

On the single European currency issue, he told reporters that the government's policies were unchanged. It will maintain its "wait-and-see" stance while acknowledging there are big obstacles to joining in the first round.
"Our position on the single currency has not changed," Brown told reporters as he unveiled his employment scheme.

Fresh uncertainty is clouding EMU after Socialist Party victory in French elections and the shelving of Bonn's plan to revalue gold reserves to help cut its budget deficit, dismissed as an accounting fiddle by the country's powerful central bank.

Sources in Chancellor Helmut Kohl's ruling coalition said the Bundesbank and German government had agreed to revalue reserves at the end of the year but not transfer the profits to Bonn until 1998, a clear victory for the central bank.

Brown's jobs plan aims to cut unemployment and increase employment opportunities and labour market flexibility across Europe. It also proposes a new task-force to help smaller firms create jobs and to push for completion of the single market.

"I intend to discuss these priorities with my Ecofin colleagues in Luxembourg on Monday. We intend to make this a key theme of our presidency of the G8 (Group of Eight) and of the European Union," he said.
But his plan did not signal a willingness to give up a veto over key issues, he said.

Britain takes up the presidency of the G8 -- the old Group of Seven industrialised nations plus Russia -- and the EU in January. Brown said he would be looking for concrete results by the end of Britain's EU presidency in a year's time.
Drawing a line under what he saw as the inertia of the previous Conservative government, Brown said his plan was the first EU initiative by a British administration for 10 years.
"No longer should the British government sit on the sidelines of Europe," he said.
For too long, he added, the EU debate had been directed only at a single European currency, due to start in January 1999. The time had come to widen it to jobs to help the people of Europe.
"Better education and higher skills, combined with reduced burdens on business, are the way to guarantee...high and stable levels of growth and unemployment.
"This is the new economic agenda. It enables us to benefit from flexible labour markets while ensuring that everyone can share in the rewards of a more dynamic economy," he said.
EU jobs and welfare rules must pass a simple test, he said -- would they increase productivity, would they raise employment opportunity and would they improve labour market flexibility?
But flexible labour markets may be resisted in countries like France where Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin has just won a stunning election victory.
In the past, his party has said it wants an immediate 500 franc ($86) hike in the monthly minimum wage and action to cut working hours while maintaining wage levels.
Brown acknowledged it may be tough to convince all his EU partners. "It will be hard in some cases to persuade people but I think we will win on this."
